sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
On 6 September 2002 an earthquake occurred on the northern Sicily offshore. The epicenter of this event lies about 40 km northeast of Palermo, coinciding with the Solunto High area. The focal mechanism shows reverse motion on NE-SW striking nodal plane. The spatial distribution of the aftershocks shows a cluster roughly trending NE-SW. All the regional centroid-moment tensor solutions computed for several events of this seismic sequence show the same thrust geometry with P axes striking from NW-SE to NNW-SSE. Similar seismic deformation has been detected in different moderate earthquakes occurred along the north Sicily offshore. This area is clearly a zone of compressive stress.
The earthquakes of the 2002 sequence are about located between 5 and 15 km. The Moho was inferred at about 22 km under the Solunto High, shallows up to 11 km northward at the continental-ocean transition, and increases to about 26 km southward under the north Sicily coast. The source of the 6 September 2002, Palermo earthquake is thought to be one of (or to lie immediately below) the thrust structures inherited from the building phase of the Sicily-Maghrebian chain (Pepe et al., 2005; Doglioni, 2007).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Was the historical seismicity along the northern coast of Sicily really due to reverse faulting offshore Sicily?
2) What is the pattern of this offshore reverse fault system?
3) Is this fault system seismogenic for its entire length?
4) Can this fault system generate a sea-bottom displacement and a possible tsunami?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Azzaro et al. (2003)
They carried out a macroseismic survey with the aim of defining the damage scenario of the September 6, 2002 earthquake. They investigated 134 localities. The seismic event, although characterised by a moderate magnitude and located about forty kilometres offshore, produced relevant macroseismic effects in the Palermo area. The earthquake has also provoked hydrological effects and slope instability processes.
Gasparini et al. (2003)
These authors investigate the peculiar macroseismic effects of the September 6, 2002 earthquake.
They analyse sounds heard during the quake, fear felt and a qualitative description of ground movement felt.
Giunta et al. (2004)
They perform a seismological analysis on a data set of about 540 seismic events which occurred in the Southern Tyrrhenian Sea from 6th September to 15th October 2002. This seismicity occurred within the Southern Tyrrhenian thinned crust, and is well clustered around a sub-horizontal regression plane dipping westwards and northwards at an average depth of about 10 km. The distribution of the hypocenters relative to this sequence emphasized the presence of a high-angle NE-SW-oriented deformation belt within which several shear surfaces are considered to be found sub-parallel to that established for the main shock.
The kinematics of all these structures is consistent with a compressive right-lateral focal mechanism.
Di Giovambattista and Tyupkin (2004)
These workers analyse seismic quiescence and accelerating seismic energy release as possible spatio-temporal patterns of the preparation of the 6 September 2002 Palermo, Italy, earthquake.
They apply the RTL algorithm. This algorithm identified a seismic quiescence started from the beginning of November 2001 and reached its minimum at the end of May 2002. The application of a log-periodic time-o-failure model gives a "predicted" (in retrospective) magnitude M=6.2 main shock on 5 May 2002.
